title: People and Teams
author: Dr. Ian Hallett
summary: In part four of his five-part Leadership Operating System series, Ian Hallett turns to the People and Teams domain, which covers supporting people, developing their capability and freedom to decide, and building a team that can disagree and perform together. He opens with Google's Project Oxygen, which set out in 2009 to show that managers did not matter, failed, and found that the best managers were coaches who empowered rather than micromanaged, with technical skill ranked last of eight behaviours. He pairs this with a meta-analysis of 136 samples linking psychological safety to role clarity, support and learning behaviour, concluding that the behaviours which make people thrive under a manager can be measured and learned. His organising test is what a team can do when the leader is absent, and he offers four ten-minute one-to-one questions covering pressure, decisions, feedback and what the team is not saying. Fifteen concrete behaviours sit behind the questions across support, development and team conditions, and he names four failure patterns of capable people: kindness without standards, the kept decision, the rescue and the loudest voice. He answers the worry that expertise becomes worthless by advising leaders to use it to ask better questions rather than supply answers.
points: The test of the People and Teams domain is what the team can do when the leader is not there, which challenges experts who were promoted on their own answers.
Four one-to-one questions (pressure, decisions, feedback, what the team is not saying) cover support, development and team conditions in about ten minutes.
Handing over a decision develops someone faster than advice, so leaders should list which decisions each report makes without asking.
Google's Project Oxygen showed that coaching, empowerment and genuine interest in people outrank technical skill, and that managers who scored badly could improve quickly.
Capable people typically fail through kindness without standards, keeping delegated decisions, rescuing instead of coaching, and letting the loudest voice stand for the team.
quotes: In 2009, a team at Google set out to answer a question the company had argued about since it was founded: do managers matter? The team expected to show they did not (engineers were sceptical of management).
First on the list was “is a good coach”. Second was “empowers the team and does not micromanage”.
My sense is that this is the domain capable operators find hardest to put first, because their expertise is what got them promoted. Being the person with the answer feels like doing the job well.
The test of this domain is what your team can do when you are not there.
The second hands over a decision, which develops someone faster than advice does.
Back people publicly when they acted reasonably. When a reasonable decision has a bad outcome, say in the meeting where it is being judged that they did what you would have done.
Development is mostly a matter of what you hand over. Every decision you keep that someone on your team could make is a lesson they do not get.
Someone brings you a problem and you solve it. We do this because it is quicker and we are good at it. The person comes back with the next one.
